title: D'accord !
subtitle: Four ways to agree
review: Written by Claude. Check the French, the English lines, the notes and the questions.
intro: A deal about the dishes, a haircut nobody noticed, a shelf built without the instructions and a morning run that turns into croissants: four short scenes between Emma and Lucas. Listen for how they say yes, and for the moments when yes means 'I don't believe you'.

lines.text: Ce soir, je cuisine et tu fais la vaisselle. D'accord ?

tr.en: Tonight, I cook and you do the washing-up. OK?

lines.note: Literally 'that works': a casual yes to an arrangement.

lines.text: Donc demain, c'est toi qui cuisines.

tr.en: So tomorrow, you're the one cooking.

lines.note: Cuisines takes -s: the verb agrees with toi.

lines.text: On est d'accord. Je commande des pizzas.

lines.note: Tricher: to cheat. La triche: cheating.

lines.text: Peut-être. Mais y aura pas de vaisselle.

tr.en: Maybe. But there won't be any washing-up.

lines.note: Y aura pas = il n'y aura pas.
Si, not oui, because the question was negative.

lines.text: Tout à fait. Exactement ce que j'allais dire.

tr.en: Quite. Exactly what I was going to say.

lines.note: La notice: the instruction leaflet. A false friend: not 'a notice'.
Il te reste…: you have … left.

lines.text: C'est vrai. Elles sont en trop.
lines.note: En trop: surplus, more than needed.
Justement turns her objection into his argument.
Drawn out and flat, c'est ça is sarcastic.

lines.text: Bon, t'as raison. Elle est où, la notice ?

tr.en: All right, you're right. Where are the instructions?
Under the shelf. To keep it level.

lines.note: Caler: to wedge something so it stops wobbling.

lines.text: Demain, je me lève à six heures pour aller courir.

tr.en: Tomorrow, I'm getting up at six to go for a run.

lines.note: She goes along with it, and makes clear she doesn't believe it.

lines.text: Sérieux ! J'ai mis le réveil. Tu viens ?

tr.en: Seriously! I've set the alarm. Are you coming?

lines.text: En fait, on pourrait commencer par les croissants.

tr.en: Actually, we could start with the croissants.

lines.note: Grave: slang for strong agreement. Le footing: a jog.

notes: D'accord says yes to a plan. Je suis d'accord agrees with an opinion. On est d'accord seals it.
Ça marche, carrément, grave and c'est clair are casual. With a boss, say tout à fait or absolument.
Si replaces oui after a negative question: Tu remarques rien ? — Si !
Tone can flip the meaning: c'est ça, oui… and si tu le dis… say 'I don't believe you'.
T'as raison gives in. Justement does the opposite: it uses the other person's point against them.
Spoken French drops ne: tu remarques rien, je porte pas, y aura pas.

questions.q: Emma proposes to swap chores tomorrow. Lucas accepts casually. What does he say?
« Tu remarques rien ? » Lucas wants to answer yes. Which word does he need?
questions.why: Si says yes to a negative question.

questions.q: Emma does not believe the leaning shelf is 'design'. What does she say?
questions.why: C'est ça, oui…, drawn out, is sarcastic: 'yeah, right'.

questions.q: Lucas suggests starting with the croissants. Emma agrees completely. What does she say?
